opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed a lot, and pretty quickly. Ten years ago, if you talked to a big enterprise about data infrastructure, the conversation was mostly about which vendor they'd pick, and they accepted that the data would live in that vendor's format. That was just how a data warehouse worked. You loaded your data in, and getting it back out was somebody else's problem later.

What's shifted is that companies got burned enough times to realize the data is the long-lived asset, and the engines on top of it come and go. So now, in a lot of the conversations I have, the very first requirement is: "Our data has to be in an open format, in our own cloud storage account, and we want to be able to point multiple engines at it." They want to run SQL with one tool, machine learning with another, maybe some new AI system next year that doesn't exist yet. They don't want to copy the data into five different silos to do that.

A few things drove it. One is the rise of the lakehouse idea, where you show you can get warehouse-style reliability and performance, with transactions, schema enforcement, and fast queries, directly on open formats like Parquet, with a table layer such as Delta Lake or Iceberg on top. Once people saw they didn't have to trade performance for openness, the calculation changed. Another is cost and governance. Keeping one copy of the data with one set of access controls is just a lot simpler than reconciling copies everywhere.

And AI has accelerated all of it. Everybody wants to use their data with models now: training, fine-tuning, retrieval, agents. They don't know exactly which tools will win, so keeping things open feels like the safe bet. The interesting part is that the competition has moved up the stack. It's less about locking in storage and more about who has the best engine, the best governance, and the best experience on top of data the customer owns. Honestly, I think that's healthier for everybody, including the vendors, because you have to keep earning the workload.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from accepting vendor-specific formats to many enterprises requiring open formats, but it does not characterize the earlier attitude as controversial or the current stance as broadly accepted.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's changed a lot, and honestly faster than I expected. When we started pushing on this at Databricks, around the time of Delta Lake and open sourcing it, the standard enterprise posture was pretty much: pick a data warehouse vendor, load everything in, and accept that the storage format is theirs. Open formats were seen as a sort of hobbyist or Hadoop-era thing. The people who cared were usually engineers who'd been burned by a migration, not the folks writing the checks.

What flipped it, I think, is a few things happening at once. One is that the cost of being locked in became very visible. Companies ended up with their data copied into three or four systems, paying to move it around, paying egress, and realizing that every new tool they wanted to adopt meant another copy. Open table formats like Delta and Iceberg basically let you keep one copy in object storage and point many engines at it, and once CFOs understood that framing, it stopped being a technical preference and became a procurement requirement. We now routinely see RFPs that say, data must be stored in an open format we control, as a hard line.

The second is AI. Everyone suddenly wanted to run new workloads, new models, new tools against the same data, and a lot of those tools didn't exist a year earlier. If your data is in a proprietary format, every one of those is a negotiation with the vendor. If it's Parquet on S3 with an open metadata layer, you can try whatever shows up on GitHub tomorrow. That really accelerated things, because the pace of change in AI made optionality feel urgent rather than theoretical.

And the third is that the vendors themselves came around, which is the part I find most interesting. A few years ago the big warehouses were very much arguing that you needed their proprietary storage for performance. Now basically all of them support reading and writing Iceberg or Delta, and they're competing on the engine rather than on holding the data hostage. We leaned into that with Delta UniForm and then with the Tabular acquisition, because the goal was always for the formats to converge enough that customers don't have to think about it. I'd say the remaining friction is less about whether enterprises want open formats and more about the catalog and governance layer on top, who controls permissions and metadata. That's the next place where I think people will insist on openness, and we've tried to get ahead of it with Unity Catalog being open source. But the basic question of whether your tables should be in a format you own, I'd say that debate is over.

r001.rationale: The response describes open formats as once dismissed as a hobbyist or Hadoop-era concern, but now broadly accepted and often required in enterprise procurement.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s been a pretty big shift. In the past, enterprises were more willing to put their data into a proprietary system and accept that they’d access it through whatever interfaces that vendor provided. Now, increasingly, they want to own the data independently of the compute engine. They want it in an open format so they can use different tools on it and aren’t locked into one vendor’s roadmap or pricing.

And it’s not necessarily because they plan to switch vendors tomorrow. It’s about preserving that option, and also being able to use multiple engines at the same time. You might have one tool that’s great for SQL analytics and another that’s great for machine learning. Having them work on the same data without making copies is really valuable.

So I think openness has gone from being a technical preference to something that comes up much earlier in enterprise buying decisions. Vendors still have to compete on performance, reliability, and ease of use, but customers increasingly expect the underlying data to remain accessible.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward greater demand for open formats and treats openness as an increasingly early buying consideration, but it does not characterize the change as moving from controversy to broad acceptance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s been a pretty big shift. In the past, enterprises were willing to put their data into a proprietary system if that system gave them the best performance or the easiest experience. Now, increasingly, they want the data itself to be in an open format, even if they’re buying a managed service to work with it.

A lot of that comes from wanting flexibility. You might have one engine that’s great for SQL, another for machine learning, and another for streaming. You don’t want to make a separate copy of your data for each one, and you don’t want changing vendors to mean migrating all your data.

So I think openness has gone from something that was nice to have to something customers explicitly ask for. They’ll still pay for performance, reliability, and management, but they want those services to compete on top of data they control.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward explicitly requested open formats, but it does not characterize the earlier attitude as controversial.
